Senses.Explanation: To take something up as one's own is to accept and stand under a presented saying, claim, capacity, or matter so that it can be used or answered for. Yuanwu Keqin joins taking it up directly with using it and acting when needed. Tianru Weize locates the matter in each listener's own share and asks for direct personal uptake; Baichi Xingyuan similarly links immediate uptake with recognizing one's own ground. Pu'an Yinsu faults people who will not take up the awakening manifest before their eyes. The same verb can expose a premature or inadequate stopping place. Hongzhi Zhengjue says one must exhaust the subtle before understanding the matter of taking-up; Micang Daokai ridicules defensive calculation about it, and Dawei Jinglun contrasts what follows a phrase with the move before the mechanism, then rebukes being caught on either side. In Xuefeng Huikong's verse, ‘Dazhi’ is Baizhang Huaihai, the titled case figure who takes it up and is deaf for three days.

Senses.Explanation: On whose grace and power is the standing question masters put to an assembly at the moment a benefit has just been tallied — grain eaten from the year's harvest, a new bell hung, a hall rebuilt by donors, a mind that does all that is needed. Hongzhi Zhengjue closes his address for the departing monastery steward with it, an unnamed monk opens Consort Wang's lecture with it, and Yuanwu Keqin presses it again at an inner-palace lecture. Dahui Zonggao plants it inside a letter as a resting place for investigation, Tianru Weize sets it at the end of a written instruction, and Xutang Zhiyu, Xisou Shaotan, and Zhufeng Zhenxu raise it over new bells, harvest stores, and a Buddha's-birthday rebuilding. At the harvest-steward addresses the question follows an inventory of what the monastery has received. Hongzhi Zhengjue recites the year of muddy farming, the grain pounded at the mill, the fragrant rice shared from a thousand bowls, asks what fills the belly — chan or rice — and ends his verse after the quoted Yaoshan line with the question and flails striking from all four sides. Xutang Zhiyu counts the great vessel of a thousand jun already raised to the tower and ten thousand hu of pearl-grain already stored, the monks entering the hall bellied and spreading their bowls, and asks it before striking his staff. Xisou Shaotan follows one grain from before the division of yin and yang to the singing walk after the meal, and asks it with a shout. At palace lectures and donor occasions the question faces the throne and the benefactors. An unnamed monk asks Consort Wang's assembled lecture — sky covering all, earth bearing the mountains and rivers — at just this moment, on whose grace and power; Yuanwu Keqin answers with one spring blossom amid a thousand flowers and adds that one must also know this grace. At an inner-palace lecture Yuanwu Keqin carries a single phrase out of the crown of a thousand sages through the whole of space as one great gate of liberation, then asks the assembly the question and answers it with the formless Buddha on the mountain of the five aggregates, lighting and shaking the sands. On the Buddha's birthday Zhufeng Zhenxu asks the question over a rebuilt seven-tiered lantern display and answers it himself: by the grace of the grand defender and the civil and military officials who gladly donated their salaries, the donors all sharing in a cause that does not wear away. In written instruction the question becomes the thread of the work itself. Dahui Zonggao tells Zhang the judicial commissioner that when all that needed doing is done, everything follows the mind with nothing lacking — just at that moment, on whose grace and power — and to keep working like this day upon day, like a man learning to shoot who naturally hits. Tianru Weize tells the trainee Zhao to set the inherited tangles aside and press hard on the one thing under investigation in every place and time — in the end, on whose grace and power. The question also opened bell ceremonies and travelled in re-edited letters. Tian'an Sheng gives the new bell its voice — no wings, yet its sound reaches the nine heavens — and asks the question over the red furnace where everything turns into a dance. The same Dahui letter that plants the question in the reply to Zhang also circulated under the title of an instruction to Zhang, the re-edition reading 'just at this moment' where the reply reads 'at this moment.'

Senses.Explanation: The Western Rank is the institutional counterpart to the Eastern Rank in a Chan monastery.
